source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (arXiv tech report of the AIJ paper)
finding: Sound, complete, best-first hitting-set diagnosis search normally needs exponential memory because all open tree paths are stored. RBF-HS adapts Korf's Recursive Best-First Search to hitting sets and enumerates a fixed number of minimal diagnoses in best-first order within linear space.
numbers: Theorem 1: time O(n + TPT) for minimum-cardinality-first and O(n^2 + TPT) for most-probable-first; space O(|K|), K = number of components/axioms.
limits: Complexity bound assumes the number of minimal conflicts is O(1). Needs a sound and complete conflict finder.
agent_relevance: Memory-bounded, best-first fault enumeration is a pattern for an agent that must list top-k suspects without storing the whole search tree.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (arXiv tech report of the AIJ paper)
finding: HBF-HS is a hybrid: run Reiter's HS-Tree while memory allows, then switch to RBF-HS, keeping soundness, completeness and best-first order.
numbers: Worst case equals the worse of RBF-HS and HS-Tree for time and space. Switch criteria tested: absolute 400 nodes in memory, and relative 60% of available memory.
limits: Worst-case bounds are not better than either parent; gains are empirical.
agent_relevance: Shows a cheap way to cap memory: do the fast thing first, fall back to the lean thing when a budget is hit.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (arXiv tech report of the AIJ paper)
finding: Benchmark: 14 real-world inconsistent or incoherent ontologies from 42 to 33,203 axioms, in description logics from ALCON(D) to SROIQ, using the Pellet reasoner. Five random target faults per setting, sequential diagnosis with split-in-half (SPL) and entropy (ENT) query selection.
numbers: Number of leading diagnoses ld in {2,6,10,20}, plus ld=100 scalability. Two preference modes: minCard and maxProb. Absolute cost per run: runtime min/avg/max 0.02/25/2176 s (ENT) and 0.03/29/4806 s (SPL); memory 7 to 2M tree nodes.
limits: Targets are random diagnoses, not real expert-intended faults; one reasoner (Pellet); ontology domain only.
agent_relevance: Describes the standard testbed that later hitting-set papers in this line reuse.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (arXiv tech report of the AIJ paper)
finding: Minimum-cardinality-first: RBF-HS saves much memory versus HS-Tree at small runtime cost. In non-trivial cases (runtime over 1 s, 94% of cases) the memory factor saved beat the time factor lost.
numbers: Mean memory saved factor 14.1 (ENT) and 13.8 (SPL), so RBF-HS used under 8% of HS-Tree memory. Factor above 10 in 45% of cases; max 50 (ENT) and 57 (SPL).
limits: In five scenarios on tiny ontologies (Koala, Cton, diagnoses of size 1) HS-Tree used slightly less memory.
agent_relevance: Space-for-time trade is favourable when problems are hard; irrelevant when they are tiny.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (arXiv tech report of the AIJ paper)
finding: RBF-HS was sometimes faster than HS-Tree despite forgetting and re-exploring, because managing the huge open-node priority queue costs time linear in depth.
numbers: Both lower runtime and large memory savings in 35% (ENT) and 38% (SPL) of cases. Worst RBF-HS overhead: factor 10.4 (ontology O, SPL, ld=20).
limits: Explanation (queue management cost) is the author's argument, not isolated experimentally here.
agent_relevance: Caution against assuming a linear-space method is always slower.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (arXiv tech report of the AIJ paper)
finding: HBF-HS repairs RBF-HS runtime overhead with a small allowance of HS-Tree work first.
numbers: With a 400-node switch, median time overhead vs HS-Tree about 0% (ENT) and 3% (SPL); faster than HS-Tree in 44% (ENT) and 42% (SPL) of the significant-overhead cases. Memory never above 416 nodes while HS-Tree needed over 500,000 nodes (factor above 1000). A 940% overhead became 2% faster (case O, SPL, 20).
limits: Extra memory after the switch was under 2% on average, max 4%.
agent_relevance: A hybrid with a hard memory cap works almost as fast as the unbounded method.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (arXiv tech report of the AIJ paper)
finding: Most-probable-first (maxProb): RBF-HS trades memory for time roughly one-to-one, a known weakness of RBFS when node f-values differ little (many 'mind shifts').
numbers: k orders of magnitude of memory saved cost about k orders of magnitude more runtime. At ld=100 RBF-HS needed up to several hours per session while HS-Tree and HBF-HS (60% switch) took a few minutes.
limits: Only HBF-HS with relative switch is recommended for maxProb; one scenario (O, SPL, 20) stayed hard even for the 400-node switch.
agent_relevance: Probability-ordered best-first is harder to make memory-light than size-ordered; avoid flat-score searches with recursion.

source: Rodler (2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (arXiv tech report of the AIJ paper)
finding: Scalability (ld=100, minCard): enormous space savings, modest time cost. Hardest cases ccc and cce come from merging two ontologies (alignment), giving many independent faults at once.
numbers: Space saved 84% (O, SPL) to above 99.9% (cce), above 95% in all but one case. Time: 9 cases overhead under 1.65x except cce at 3.18x (SPL) and 2.09x (ENT); 5 cases faster by 7 to 22%. Hardest cases: space saved up to nearly 4 orders of magnitude; in 3 of 5 ENT runs on cce HS-Tree ran out of memory while RBF-HS used at most 102 nodes in about 2.5 min; ccc, ENT, 2: HS-Tree used over 800x the memory, RBF-HS 3% faster.
limits: Alignment cases have large-cardinality diagnoses (up to size 16 to 35 in some ontologies), so trees get deep.
agent_relevance: Large-cardinality multi-fault cases are where memory-light search matters most; relevant if an agent faces many simultaneous errors.

source: Rodler (2022) Sound, Complete, Linear-Space, Best-First Diagnosis Search (arXiv short version of RBF-HS)
finding: Earlier short version tested only minimum-cardinality tasks on ten cases.
numbers: Memory savings up to 98%; in four of ten cases runtime also lower, with runtime savings up to above 88%.
limits: Smaller benchmark than the full report; headline memory figure (98%) rises to above 99.9% in the later full report.
agent_relevance: Check numbers across versions: headline figures grew as the benchmark grew.

source: Rodler (2021/2022) DynamicHS: Streamlining Reiter's Hitting-Set Tree for Sequential Diagnosis
finding: Reiter (1987) asked whether the HS-Tree computed for old diagnoses can be reused after a new measurement. Standard practice discards and rebuilds the tree each iteration. DynamicHS keeps state and minimises reasoner calls, answering that question.
numbers: Keeps the tree across the session, with lazy updates and cheaper set operations replacing expensive reasoner calls.
quote: reuse an existing search tree to compute fault explanations after new system information is obtained
limits: Statefulness costs memory; needs the sequential setting where the problem changes by added measurements.
agent_relevance: Keeping the hypothesis tree between tests, instead of rebuilding it, maps to an agent that reuses its earlier reasoning when new evidence arrives.

source: Rodler (2021/2022) DynamicHS
finding: Benchmark of 20 real-world faulty ontologies; 20 sequential sessions per scenario; scenarios vary ld and measurement heuristic (ENT, SPL, MPS). DynamicHS faster than HS-Tree in almost all.
numbers: Less runtime than HS-Tree in 99.4% of scenarios and 96% of single sessions (96% all, 96% ENT, 97% SPL, 95% MPS). Median and max savings 52% and 75%; HS-Tree needs up to 4x the time on average and over 9x in single sessions.
limits: Median savings independent of ld and heuristic. Both compute identical diagnoses. The thesis and journal quote 99.4% of scenarios; the arXiv abstract quotes 96% of sessions.
agent_relevance: Same answers, fewer reasoner calls: the gain is engineering, not approximation.

source: Rodler (2021/2022) DynamicHS
finding: Hardest cases gain more. The hardest session per scenario was up to one order of magnitude harder than average.
numbers: Savings in hardest cases: median 60%/60%/70% (ENT/SPL/MPS), max 86%/86%/89%; abstract says median 64% and max 89%, and avoided median time overheads of over 175% and max 800%. Hardest-case savings exceeded median savings in 83% of scenarios.
limits: Per-scenario sample is 20 sessions.
agent_relevance: Statefulness pays most when the problem is hard.

source: Rodler (2021/2022) DynamicHS
finding: Memory cost of statefulness is moderate.
numbers: DynamicHS used less memory than HS-Tree in 14% of scenarios, under 25% overhead in 35%, under 50% in 52%, and under twice HS-Tree memory in 82%. In two thirds of scenarios the memory factor was smaller than the node-processing factor saved. Duplicate nodes were under 10% of memory.
limits: Whenever HS-Tree fit in memory in the experiments, DynamicHS did too.
agent_relevance: Time versus space is the main axis of the field; DynamicHS and RBF-HS sit at opposite ends.

source: Rodler (2019) Towards Optimizing Reiter's HS-Tree for Sequential Diagnosis
finding: Workshop-length first version of DynamicHS. States that no algorithm had answered Reiter's question on tree reuse, and that existing sequential debuggers re-invoke HS-Tree from scratch each time.
numbers: Preliminary evaluation only; reported significant time savings from fewer reasoner calls.
limits: Preliminary results; full numbers appear in the 2020/2022 version.
agent_relevance: Shows a 32-year gap between Reiter's 1987 question and an answer.

source: Rodler & Elichanova (2020/2022) Do We Really Sample Right in Model-Based Diagnosis?
finding: Sequential diagnosis uses a sample of diagnoses to choose the next measurement. Best-first samples are biased, yet standard. Six sample types were compared on 8 problems, 5 sample sizes and 4 heuristics (240 cases in EXP1, 960 in EXP2).
numbers: Random samples estimate better statistically (random best or second best for elimination rate in 100% of cases, best in 75%). Best-first best or second best for probability estimates in all but one case (63% best, 25% second). In practice best-first needed fewest measurements for ENT and SPL but was worst for MPS: 58 measurements vs 25 with random (problem U, k=50).
quote: a generally most favorable sampling technique cannot be nominated
limits: Better statistical representativeness did not imply better practical performance. Larger samples did not reliably cut measurements. Only small ontologies where all minimal diagnoses can be generated. No single best sampler.
agent_relevance: If an agent samples hypotheses to pick the next test, top-candidates sampling is a sound default but heuristic-dependent; sample sizes above about 10 give diminishing returns.

source: Rodler & Elichanova (2020/2022) Do We Really Sample Right
finding: Time-versus-information tradeoff in sampling: when sampling is cheapest, the resulting measurements are less informative.
numbers: Guidance from Table 4: sample size below 10 use best-first; 10 use approximate best-first; 20 use approximate worst-first if measuring is cheap, else best-first; 50 use random if an efficient method exists; ENT and SPL best-first; MPS approximate random.
limits: Brute-force random sampling in the experiments, so sampling-time rankings depend on implementation.
agent_relevance: Choose the sampling method by how costly each real test is.

source: Rodler (2023) Don't Treat the Symptom, Find the Cause! (habilitation thesis summarising his efficient-diagnosis research)
finding: Thesis restates headline results of RBF-HS and DynamicHS and adds other efficiency lines.
numbers: RBF-HS: in one case HS-Tree ran out of memory at 32 GB while RBF-HS never stored more than 125 tree nodes; in another case 65% runtime saving with 99.9% memory reduction.
limits: Written by the algorithm author; self-reported. No independent replication found in this session.
agent_relevance: One lab authored most of the efficient-hitting-set evidence; treat as a single group's results.

source: Rodler (2023) habilitation thesis, query synthesis chapter
finding: Query synthesis (QS) computes the best next query without enumerating a query pool.
numbers: QS reached above 99.999% of theoretically optimal query value in under 1 s, exploring under 4% of query space; handled up to 80 diagnoses where pool-based selection (PB) managed about 10 within an hour; PB needed 27/787/2528 times (min/avg/max) QS time (PB 6/137/566 s vs QS never above 0.6 s).
limits: Marked preliminary results in the thesis.
agent_relevance: Efficient choice of the best next test matters as much as fast hypothesis search.

source: Rodler (2023) habilitation thesis, heuristic study chapter
finding: Query-selection heuristic choice depends on quality of the fault-probability information.
numbers: A wrong heuristic costs avg/max 100%/250% extra oracle effort. Misleading priors: random selection best. Vague priors: MPS best. Reasonable priors: BME best, then entropy and EMCb. No universal best heuristic.
limits: Prior study on real-world cases; priors manipulated by the author.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a prior blindly: with bad priors, random probing beats clever probing.

source: Rodler (2023) habilitation thesis, user-study chapter (Rodler, Jannach, Schekotihin, Fleiss 2019, KBS)
finding: First user study of query-based ontology debugging versus manual test-case debugging, with trained CS students using OntoDebug.
numbers: Manual approach overhead averaged 37% in time and 117% in mouse-click effort, with no loss in fault-finding effectiveness for the query-based approach.
limits: Students, not ontology professionals; only the thesis summary was read, not the original paper.
agent_relevance: A system that asks well-chosen yes/no questions saves human effort.

source: Rodler (2023) habilitation thesis, randomised scheduling chapter (Rodler, Teppan, Jannach 2021, KR)
finding: Optimisation by randomisation: generate many random minimal diagnoses with QuickXplain and keep the best, instead of asking a solver for the optimal diagnosis.
numbers: In over-constrained scheduling, better diagnoses in under half the time of a leading solver in all cases; 25% on average and 60% at most fewer product orders cancelled or postponed. A reasoner call takes up to minutes; direct optimisation takes hours.
limits: Scheduling benchmarks, not logic debugging; thesis summary only.
agent_relevance: Random restarts plus cheap minimisation can beat exact optimisation when each check is expensive.

source: Rodler (2023) habilitation thesis, spreadsheet chapter
finding: Abstract spreadsheet models versus an exact value-based model for diagnosis.
numbers: Abstract models were 1 to over 4 orders of magnitude faster on average; the qualitative deviation model matched exact-model accuracy in a third of cases and up to over half per scenario.
limits: The exact model is often not applicable at all.
agent_relevance: Coarser models trade a little accuracy for large speed.

source: Rodler (2022/2024) How should I compute my candidates? A taxonomy and classification of diagnosis computation algorithms
finding: Taxonomy of 12 features (soundness, completeness, best-first, multiple solutions, way of conflict computation, stateful or stateless, black-box reasoning, general applicability, space efficiency and others). Table 1 classifies HS-DAG (1989), STACCATO (2009), SAT-based (2014), Parallel HS-Tree (2016), DynamicHS (2020), HBF-HS (2022).
numbers: Space efficiency is defined as polynomial worst-case memory. The paper says only few space-efficient strategies exist.
limits: Author's own classification; list explicitly incomplete.
agent_relevance: A checklist for picking a search method for an agent's fault hypotheses.

source: Rodler (2022/2024) taxonomy
finding: Dropping soundness, completeness or best-first improves speed but adds risk: unsound methods may return non-minimal sets, and losing best-first removes the guarantee that the actual fault is located efficiently. Duality property: X is a diagnosis iff the components outside X are not a hitting set of the minimal conflicts.
numbers: Qualitative; no experiments.
limits: No measured comparison.
agent_relevance: Matches the schema idea that locating a fault by code needs complete enumeration where safety matters.

source: Shchekotykhin, Fleiss, Rodler, Friedrich (2012) Direct computation of diagnoses for ontology debugging (INV-HS-Tree)
finding: Computes diagnoses directly with Inv-QuickXplain, a divide-and-conquer over the diagnosis set, skipping conflict-set precomputation which is infeasible for aligned ontologies with many conflicts.
numbers: OAEI 2011 Conference track: 286 alignments, 140 consistent and coherent, 122 incoherent, 26 inconsistent. Of 146 faulty ones, both methods handled 133 for 1, 9 and 30 diagnoses; in 13 cases only INV-HS-Tree finished (HS-Tree found only 1 diagnosis in 2 hours for csa-conference-ekaw). Anatomy track (11545 and 4838 axioms plus 1147 to 1461 alignment axioms): target diagnosis in about 40 s on average, INV-HS-Tree slightly ahead of HS-Tree. Conference: one minimal diagnosis in about 25 s.
limits: Direct method wins mainly when 1 diagnosis is requested; the gap shrinks for 9 and 30.
agent_relevance: Skipping explicit conflicts is another way to cope with many simultaneous faults.

source: Rodler (2023) habilitation thesis on QuickXplain (Junker 2004) and Rodler 2020 proof
finding: QuickXplain finds an irreducible subset with a monotone property by divide and conquer using a linear number of consistency checks. It sits inside most conflict-based diagnosers and in randomised diagnosis sampling. The thesis says no formal correctness proof was published until Rodler 2020 (arXiv 2001.01835).
numbers: Linear number of consistency checks; the thesis says a study confirmed people find it hard to understand.
limits: Secondary description via the thesis; QuickXplain itself not opened.
agent_relevance: QuickXplain is a recipe for finding a minimal failing subset of steps with few checks.

source: Rodler (2023) habilitation thesis intro on Reiter's HS-Tree (Reiter 1987; Greiner, Smith, Wilkerson 1989)
finding: Reiter (1987) A Theory of Diagnosis from First Principles is the founding paper: diagnoses are minimal hitting sets of conflicts, computed with an HS-Tree. HS-DAG (1989) repaired the original tree.
numbers: About 4500 Google Scholar citations by December 2022.
limits: The 1987 and 1989 papers were not opened; facts come via the thesis and taxonomy table.
agent_relevance: Founding algorithm for S5-style fault location.

source: Hipler, Leucker, Rodler (2026) A Unified Framework for Runtime Verification and Model-Based Diagnosis in Lola
finding: Recent work embeds model-based diagnosis in a stream-based runtime verification language, with uncertainty and temporal diagnosis. Hitting-set diagnosis is still active.
numbers: No benchmark numbers read; only abstract and introduction.
limits: Not an LLM study and no efficiency data read.
agent_relevance: The diagnosis line is moving toward live monitoring.

source: Search note (this session): arXiv listing queries for LLM plus hitting-set, MUS, QuickXplain, ontology-repair diagnosis
finding: No LLM study that tests or uses RBF-HS, DynamicHS or other efficient hitting-set diagnosis was found. WebSearch budget was exhausted and Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors, so absence is not proof.
numbers: 0 LLM studies found.
limits: Search tools were limited.
agent_relevance: Gap: no measured LLM results to import; treat the algorithm results as design guidance only.
